paragraphs.paraphrase: Odysseus answers King Alcinous, his host at a feast. He praises the bard's singing and says there is no finer sight than a whole community feasting together while a servant pours wine for everyone. But since the king has asked him to tell of his sufferings, he hardly knows where to begin, because the gods have treated him harshly.

barriers.quote: King Alcinous
barriers.my_reading: the king who is hosting Odysseus at this feast
barriers.note: this Book does not say where they are or who Alcinous's people are; it relies on earlier Books

barriers.quote: the cup-bearer draws wine and fills his cup for every man
barriers.my_reading: a servant draws wine from the bowl and fills each guest's cup in turn
barriers.note: 'his cup' can be read as the cup-bearer's own cup

paragraphs.paraphrase: He reveals his name so that his hosts may one day be his guests in return, although he lives far away: he is Odysseus, son of Laertes, famous for his cunning. He describes his home, Ithaca, a rugged island among a group of neighboring islands that breeds brave men, and says that although the goddesses Calypso and Circe each kept him and wanted to marry him, he refused, because nothing matters more than home and parents. He now begins the story of his troubled voyage home from Troy.

barriers.quote: so that you too may know it, and one day, if I outlive this time of sorrow, may become my guests
barriers.my_reading: once they know who he is, they can visit him and be his guests, returning the hospitality they are showing him now
barriers.note: the link between telling his name and their becoming his guests is implied, not explained

barriers.quote: renowned among mankind for all manner of subtlety
barriers.my_reading: famous for cunning, cleverness and tricks
barriers.note: modern 'subtlety' suggests nuance or delicacy rather than craftiness

barriers.quote: Ithaca lies low on the horizon, farthest out to sea toward the sunset, while the others lie away from it toward the dawn
barriers.my_reading: Ithaca is the westernmost island of the group and the others lie east of it; 'lies low' seems to mean it looks low from the sea
barriers.note: 'lies low' seems to contradict the 'high mountain' just mentioned; sunset/dawn stand for west/east

barriers.quote: my eyes know none they would rather look upon
barriers.my_reading: there is no place he would rather see than Ithaca
barriers.note: 'none' could refer to the brave men or to places

barriers.quote: the cunning Aeaean goddess Circe
barriers.my_reading: Circe, a goddess from a place presumably called Aeaea
barriers.note: 'Aeaean' is unexplained, and Circe has not been introduced

paragraphs.paraphrase: Sailing from Troy, Odysseus and his men reached Ismarus, city of the Cicons; they sacked it, killed the people, carried off the women and loot and shared it fairly. He urged them to leave at once, but the men foolishly stayed to drink and slaughter animals on the beach, while the Cicons called in more numerous and better-trained neighbors from inland. These attacked next morning in huge numbers; the Greeks held out until the afternoon but were then beaten, losing six men from each ship, and fled with the survivors.

barriers.quote: bronze-shod spears
barriers.my_reading: spears with bronze tips

barriers.quote: toward the time when men unyoke their oxen
barriers.my_reading: late afternoon, when farmers finish ploughing and release their oxen
barriers.note: old rural way of telling the time

paragraphs.paraphrase: They sailed on, grieving but relieved, after first calling out three times to each of the men killed by the Cicons. Zeus sent a violent north-wind storm that blacked out land and sky and ripped their sails, so they lowered them and rowed to shore, where they lay for two days in misery. On the third day they sailed again, and Odysseus would have reached home, but wind and currents drove him off course as he rounded Cape Malea near the island of Cythera.

barriers.quote: called three times upon each one of the poor fellows who had died
barriers.my_reading: they shouted each dead man's name three times as a farewell or ritual before leaving
barriers.note: the purpose of this ritual is not explained

barriers.quote: night came down out of the heavens
barriers.my_reading: the storm clouds made it as dark as night even in daytime

barriers.quote: We let the ships run before the gale
barriers.my_reading: they let the storm wind drive the ships along from behind
barriers.note: sailing term

barriers.quote: I should have got home unharmed then had not the north wind and the currents been against me
barriers.my_reading: I would have got home safely if the wind and currents had not been against me
barriers.note: 'should' in the old sense of 'would', plus the inverted 'had not'

paragraphs.paraphrase: After nine days of bad winds they reached the land of the Lotus-eaters and landed for water and a meal. Odysseus sent two men, with a third as their attendant, to find out about the inhabitants; the Lotus-eaters were friendly and gave them lotus to eat, which made them lose all wish to go home or even report back. Odysseus dragged the weeping men back to the ships, tied them under the rowing benches, and hurried everyone else aboard before anyone else could eat it.

barriers.quote: they had a third man under them
barriers.my_reading: a third, lower-ranking man went with them as an attendant
barriers.note: 'under them' can momentarily be read physically

barriers.quote: were for staying
barriers.my_reading: wanted to stay
barriers.note: old British idiom

barriers.quote: made them fast under the benches
barriers.my_reading: tied them up beneath the rowing benches
barriers.note: 'made fast' = tied securely; nautical/archaic

paragraphs.paraphrase: They reached the land of the Cyclopes, a lawless, savage people who do no farming but live off wheat, barley and grapes (which give them wine) that grow wild without cultivation. They have no laws or public meetings; each lives with his own family in a cave on a mountain top, ruling it himself and ignoring his neighbors.

barriers.quote: without any kind of tillage
barriers.my_reading: without any ploughing or cultivation

barriers.quote: their wild grapes yield them wine as the sun and the rain may bring them on
barriers.my_reading: their wild grapes, ripened by sun and rain, give them wine without any effort on their part
barriers.note: unclear how wine comes without winemaking; 'bring them on' = ripen them

paragraphs.paraphrase: Off the Cyclopes' harbor lies a fertile, wooded island full of undisturbed wild goats: no hunters go there and no one farms it, because the Cyclopes have no ships or shipbuilders to reach it. Odysseus describes how good it would be for settlers (meadows, vines, deep ploughland), and says its harbor is so sheltered that ships need no ropes or anchors, only to be pulled up on the beach until a good wind comes; at its head a spring flows from a cave, ringed with poplars.

barriers.quote: sportsmen—who as a rule will suffer so much hardship in forest or among mountain precipices—do not go there
barriers.my_reading: hunters, who normally put up with any hardship to hunt, never go to this island
barriers.note: 'sportsmen' in the old sense of hunters; the reason they stay away comes only in the following sentences

barriers.quote: no cables are wanted
barriers.my_reading: no mooring ropes are needed
barriers.note: 'wanted' = needed; 'cables' = ropes

barriers.quote: till the wind becomes fair for putting out to sea again
barriers.my_reading: until the wind is favorable for sailing
barriers.note: 'fair' = favorable

paragraphs.paraphrase: They arrived at this island on a pitch-dark, misty, moonless night, so dark that a god must have guided them; there were no waves breaking on a shore to warn them, and they only knew they had arrived when they ran onto the beach. They beached the ships, lowered the sails and slept on the shore until dawn.

barriers.quote: there were no breakers to tell us we were close in shore
barriers.my_reading: there were no waves breaking on the beach to warn them that land was near

barriers.quote: Here we came in
barriers.my_reading: they landed on the goat island just described, not on the Cyclopes' mainland
barriers.note: confirmed only in the next paragraph

paragraphs.paraphrase: At dawn they explored the island; nymphs stirred up the wild goats and the men hunted them with spears and bows in three groups, getting nine goats for each of the twelve ships and ten for Odysseus's own. They feasted all day on goat meat and on wine captured from the Cicons, looking across at the nearby land of the Cyclopes, where they saw smoke and could almost hear voices and flocks. That night they slept on the beach, and next morning Odysseus called a meeting.

barriers.quote: When Dawn, the rosy-fingered child of morning, appeared
barriers.my_reading: at sunrise; dawn is pictured as a goddess whose fingers are the pink rays of early light
barriers.note: 'child of morning' is puzzling, since dawn is the start of morning; the formula recurs several times

barriers.quote: the nymphs, daughters of Zeus, roused the wild goats
barriers.my_reading: minor nature goddesses startled the goats out of cover so the men could hunt them

barriers.quote: Heaven sent us excellent sport
barriers.my_reading: the gods gave them very good hunting
barriers.note: 'sport' = hunting

barriers.quote: the livelong day
barriers.my_reading: the whole day long
barriers.note: archaic; recurs

barriers.quote: the smoke of their stubble fires
barriers.my_reading: smoke from fires, apparently burning dry stalks or brush
barriers.note: stubble suggests harvested fields, but ¶5 says the Cyclopes neither plant nor plow

paragraphs.paraphrase: Odysseus tells the rest of the men to stay on the island while he takes his own ship across to find out whether the Cyclopes are savages or hospitable, civilized people.

Odysseus and his crew rowed the short distance and saw, near the sea, a large cave in a cliff shaded by laurel trees, used as a fold for many sheep and goats, with a big walled yard in front made of stones and pine and oak trunks. It was the home of a huge, solitary, lawless monster, away with his flocks at the time, who looked less like a man than like a lone rocky mountain peak.

barriers.quote: loose the hawsers
barriers.my_reading: untie the mooring ropes
barriers.note: 'hawsers' is a specialist nautical word; the phrase recurs

barriers.quote: It was a station for a great many sheep and goats
barriers.my_reading: it was a shelter or fold where many sheep and goats were kept

barriers.quote: a high wall round it made of stones built into the ground and of trees, both pine and oak
barriers.my_reading: a wall of stones set into the ground, with pine and oak trunks built into it
barriers.note: hard to picture how trees form part of the wall

barriers.quote: resembling rather some crag that stands out boldly against the sky on the top of a high mountain
barriers.my_reading: he looked like a huge jagged rock on a mountain top: massive, rough and alone
barriers.note: the Book never actually describes his body or face

paragraphs.paraphrase: Leaving the crew with the ship, Odysseus took his twelve best men and a goatskin of strong dark wine. The wine had been a gift from Maron, a priest of Apollo at Ismarus whom Odysseus's men had spared along with his wife and child; Maron gave him gold, a silver bowl and twelve jars of this wine, which was so strong that Maron diluted it twenty to one and still its smell was irresistible. Odysseus brought it, with food, because he suspected they would meet some powerful savage who respected no law.

barriers.quote: a goatskin of sweet black wine
barriers.my_reading: a wine bag made of goat hide, filled with dark red wine
barriers.note: 'black wine' recurs

barriers.quote: seven talents of fine gold
barriers.my_reading: a large amount of gold, measured in a unit of weight or money called a talent
barriers.note: modern 'talent' means skill

barriers.quote: the wooded precincts of the temple
barriers.my_reading: the wooded grounds around the temple

barriers.quote: twelve jars of sweet wine, unmixed
barriers.my_reading: undiluted wine; apparently wine was normally mixed with water before drinking
barriers.note: the custom is only partly explained by the next sentence

barriers.quote: I filled a large skin with this wine
barriers.my_reading: this is the same goatskin mentioned at the start of the paragraph, after the digression about Maron
barriers.note: reads as if a second skin is being filled

barriers.quote: my mind misgave me
barriers.my_reading: I had a foreboding
barriers.note: archaic

paragraphs.paraphrase: The Cyclops was out, so they entered his cave and looked around: racks full of cheeses, pens crammed with lambs and young goats sorted by age, and dairy vessels brimming with whey. The men begged Odysseus to steal some cheeses and animals and sail off at once; he admits that would have been wiser, but he refused because he wanted to meet the owner and hoped for a gift, and the meeting turned out badly for his men.

barriers.quote: lambs and kids
barriers.my_reading: young sheep and young goats
barriers.note: 'kids' may briefly suggest children, especially when heard aloud

barriers.quote: first the yearlings, then the oldest of the younger lambs, and last the very young ones
barriers.my_reading: the animals were penned in three age groups: year-old ones, older young ones, and newborns

barriers.quote: all swimming with whey
barriers.my_reading: full to the brim with whey, the watery liquid left over from milk or cheese-making

barriers.quote: in the hope that he might give me a present
barriers.my_reading: he expected the owner to give a visiting stranger the customary gift of hospitality
barriers.note: the custom of guest-gifts is implied, not explained; the motive can read as simple greed

paragraphs.paraphrase: They lit a fire, burned some cheese as an offering to the gods, ate some, and waited. The Cyclops came home with a huge load of firewood and threw it down with a crash that sent them hiding at the back of the cave; he brought in the females for milking (leaving the males in the yard) and closed the entrance with a stone too heavy for twenty-two wagons to move. He milked the animals, let the young suckle, set half the milk to curdle for cheese and kept half to drink, then lit his fire, spotted the men and spoke.

barriers.quote: offered some of the cheeses in sacrifice
barriers.my_reading: burned some of the cheese in the fire as an offering to the gods
barriers.note: how one sacrifices cheese is not described

barriers.quote: let each of them have her own young
barriers.my_reading: let each mother animal suckle her own lamb or kid
barriers.note: recurs

barriers.quote: He curdled half the milk and set it aside in wicker strainers
barriers.my_reading: he turned half the milk into curds for cheese and put them in woven baskets to drain

paragraphs.paraphrase: The Cyclops asks the strangers who they are and where they sail from: are they traders, or pirates who raid everyone and are everyone's enemy?

barriers.quote: do you sail the sea as rovers, with your hands against every man and every man’s hand against you
barriers.my_reading: are you pirates who attack everyone and are attacked by everyone
barriers.note: 'rovers' = sea-raiders; biblical-sounding phrasing

paragraphs.paraphrase: Terrified, Odysseus says they are Achaeans sailing home from Troy, blown off course by Zeus and the weather, and followers of Agamemnon, son of Atreus, whose sack of that great city made him famous. He humbly asks for hospitality and the gifts guests can expect, and warns the Cyclops to fear the gods, since they are suppliants and Zeus protects and avenges travelers and suppliants.

barriers.quote: We are Achaeans
barriers.my_reading: the Greeks who fought at Troy
barriers.note: the name is never explained; that it means Greeks is outside knowledge only, though 'on our way home from Troy' helps

barriers.quote: We are the people of Agamemnon, son of Atreus
barriers.my_reading: they fought under Agamemnon, the commander of the army that sacked Troy
barriers.note: who Agamemnon is, and why Odysseus, a king himself, calls himself one of his people, is not explained here

barriers.quote: we are your suppliants
barriers.my_reading: they are formally begging for his protection and mercy, which under Zeus's law he must grant
barriers.note: 'suppliant' is an uncommon word and implies a custom the reader may not know

paragraphs.paraphrase: The Cyclops answers that Odysseus must be a fool, or a stranger to this land, to tell him to fear the gods: the Cyclopes care nothing for Zeus or any god because they are stronger, and he will spare no one out of respect for Zeus unless he feels like it. Then he asks where their ship is moored: around the headland, or close by?

barriers.quote: Was it round the point, or is she lying straight off the land?
barriers.my_reading: is your ship moored around the headland, or just offshore right here
barriers.note: 'the point' = headland; 'she' = the ship

paragraphs.paraphrase: Seeing that the Cyclops was trying to trick him into revealing where the ship was, Odysseus lied: he said Poseidon had wrecked their ship on rocks at the far end of the land and that only he and these men had survived.

barriers.quote: He said this to draw me out
barriers.my_reading: the question was a trick to learn where the ship and the other men were, presumably so he could attack them or cut off their escape
barriers.note: the Cyclops's motive is left for the reader to infer

paragraphs.paraphrase: Without a word the Cyclops seized two of the men, smashed them on the ground like puppies, tore them apart and ate them whole, then drank milk and fell asleep among his sheep while the others wept and prayed. Odysseus wanted to stab him in his sleep but realized that, with the Cyclops dead, no one could move the huge stone from the doorway and they would all be trapped, so they waited in misery until morning.

barriers.quote: a drink of neat milk
barriers.my_reading: plain, undiluted milk
barriers.note: 'neat' in the sense of unmixed; a modern reader may read 'tidy'

paragraphs.paraphrase: In the morning the Cyclops did his milking, ate two more men for breakfast, rolled the stone aside with ease to let the flocks out and put it back as lightly as fitting a lid on a quiver, trapping the Greeks inside. He shouted his flocks up the mountain, leaving Odysseus to plot revenge and glory.

barriers.quote: as easily as though he were merely clapping the lid on a quiver full of arrows
barriers.my_reading: moving the huge stone was as easy for him as snapping the cap onto an arrow case
barriers.note: a quiver with a lid is not a familiar object

barriers.quote: milked his goats and ewes, all quite properly
barriers.my_reading: he did his milking in the correct, orderly way, like a careful herdsman
barriers.note: the repeated 'quite properly' seems ironic, but its point is unclear

paragraphs.paraphrase: Odysseus's plan: the Cyclops had a huge club of freshly cut olive wood, as big as the mast of a large ship, which he was letting dry to use as a staff. Odysseus cut off about six feet, had his men smooth it, sharpened the end himself, hardened it in the fire and hid it under the dung; the men drew lots, and four were chosen to help him drive it into the Cyclops's eye while he slept. That evening the Cyclops brought all his animals inside, did his milking, ate two more men, and Odysseus approached him with a bowl of the dark wine.

barriers.quote: green olive wood
barriers.my_reading: freshly cut, not yet dried olive wood
barriers.note: 'green' means unseasoned, not the color; the rest of the sentence helps

barriers.quote: a twenty-oared merchant ship of large burden
barriers.my_reading: a large cargo ship rowed with twenty oars
barriers.note: 'burden' = carrying capacity

barriers.quote: The lot fell on the very four I should have chosen
barriers.my_reading: the draw happened to pick exactly the four men I would have picked myself
barriers.note: 'should' = would

barriers.quote: bore it into the monster’s eye
barriers.my_reading: the Cyclops has a single eye, so blinding it blinds him completely
barriers.note: the Book never says he has only one eye; general/outside knowledge only

barriers.quote: some fancy must have taken him
barriers.my_reading: he must have had a sudden whim

paragraphs.paraphrase: Odysseus offers the Cyclops the wine, saying he brought it as a gift in the hope of pity and help getting home, and scolds him for eating his guests: who will ever visit him if he behaves like this?

barriers.quote: as a drink offering
barriers.my_reading: as a gift of wine, the kind poured out in honor of a god

barriers.quote: ramping and raving intolerably
barriers.my_reading: raging and ranting unbearably
barriers.note: 'ramping' is unusual

paragraphs.paraphrase: The Cyclops drinks, loves it and asks for more, asking Odysseus's name at once and promising him a gift; he says his own land grows wine grapes, but this tastes like the drink and food of the gods combined.

barriers.quote: this drinks like nectar and ambrosia all in one
barriers.my_reading: it tastes as good as the food and drink of the gods
barriers.note: 'ambrosia' is not explained

paragraphs.paraphrase: Odysseus refills the bowl three times; once the Cyclops is drunk, he tells him, as a trick, that his name is 'Noman' and asks for the promised gift.

barriers.quote: My name is Noman
barriers.my_reading: a false name that sounds like 'no man' (nobody), set up for a later trick
barriers.note: its purpose becomes clear only at ¶27; aloud it is heard as 'no man'

paragraphs.paraphrase: The Cyclops replies cruelly that his gift to Noman will be to eat him last, after all his companions.

The drunken Cyclops falls asleep on his back, vomiting wine and bits of the men. Odysseus heats the sharpened stake in the embers until it glows and, with his four men, drives it into the Cyclops's eye, twisting it like a shipbuilder's drill while the blood boils and the eye hisses like hot iron plunged into water. The Cyclops screams, tears out the stake and yells for the neighboring Cyclopes, who gather outside the cave to ask what is wrong.

barriers.quote: gobbets of human flesh
barriers.my_reading: lumps of human flesh

barriers.quote: boring a hole in a ship’s plank with an auger that two men with a wheel and strap can keep turning
barriers.my_reading: like a carpenter's drill spun by two men pulling a strap wound around it
barriers.note: hard to picture the tool; 'auger' and 'wheel and strap' are unfamiliar

barriers.quote: all besmirched with gore
barriers.my_reading: covered in blood
barriers.note: archaic

barriers.quote: made the cave ring again
barriers.my_reading: made the cave echo
barriers.note: 'again' = back, echoing, not 'a second time'

barriers.quote: We ran away in a fright
barriers.my_reading: they retreated into the depths of the cave, since the stone still blocked the exit
barriers.note: they cannot actually leave the cave

paragraphs.paraphrase: The other Cyclopes call to Polyphemus (the first time the Cyclops is named), asking why he is shouting and keeping them awake: surely no one is stealing his sheep or trying to kill him by trickery or force?

barriers.quote: either by fraud or by force
barriers.my_reading: by trickery or by violence
barriers.note: 'fraud' in the old sense of deceit

paragraphs.paraphrase: Polyphemus shouts that Noman is killing him by trickery, not by force, which his neighbors hear as 'no man is killing me'.

barriers.quote: Noman is killing me by fraud; no man is killing me by force.
barriers.my_reading: he means 'Noman (Odysseus) is killing me by trickery, not by force', but the others hear 'nobody is killing me'
barriers.note: the pun depends on the capital N on the page; aloud 'Noman' and 'no man' sound identical, so the two halves are hard to tell apart

paragraphs.paraphrase: The neighbors conclude that if no one is attacking him he must be ill, which is Zeus's doing and cannot be helped, and advise him to pray to his father, Poseidon.

The neighbors leave, and Odysseus laughs to himself at his trick. The blinded Cyclops, groaning, gropes his way to the door, removes the stone, and sits in the entrance with his hands spread out to catch anyone trying to slip out among the sheep.

Desperate, Odysseus devises an escape: he silently ties the big, thick-fleeced rams together in threes with willow twigs from the Cyclops's bed, so that a man clings under the middle ram of each trio, shielded by the two outer ones. He himself grips the finest ram and hangs face-up beneath its belly, holding tight to the thick wool.

They waited in fear all night. At dawn the rams hurried out to pasture while the unmilked ewes bleated in the pens; the Cyclops, despite his pain, felt the backs of the animals as they passed but never thought to feel underneath. The big ram carrying Odysseus came out last, and Polyphemus stopped it and spoke to it.

barriers.quote: felt the backs of all the sheep as they stood upright
barriers.my_reading: he ran his hands over their backs as they walked past on their feet
barriers.note: 'stood upright' is an odd phrase for sheep

paragraphs.paraphrase: Polyphemus asks his favorite ram why, unlike its habit of leading the flock out first and coming home first, it is lagging behind today: is it grieving because its master was made drunk and blinded by Noman and his crew? He vows to kill Noman, and wishes the ram could talk and tell him where Noman is hiding so he could smash his brains out.

barriers.quote: got him down in his drink and blinded him
barriers.my_reading: overpowered me while I was drunk and blinded me; the Cyclops is speaking of himself as 'your master' and 'him'
barriers.note: third-person self-reference makes 'him' momentarily unclear

paragraphs.paraphrase: Once outside, a little way from the cave, Odysseus let go of the ram, freed his men, and they drove the fat flock down to the ship. The crew rejoiced to see them but mourned those who had been eaten; Odysseus signaled them to be quiet, load the sheep and put to sea, and they rowed off. When they were just within shouting range, he began taunting the Cyclops.
Odysseus shouts that the Cyclops should have judged his opponent better before eating his men; eating one's guests is a crime, and now Zeus and the other gods have punished him for it.

barriers.quote: you should have taken better measure of your man
barriers.my_reading: you should have sized up your opponent better

paragraphs.paraphrase: Enraged, the Cyclops ripped the top off a mountain and hurled it; it landed just by the ship, nearly hitting the steering oar, and the wave it raised swept them back toward the shore. Odysseus pushed off with a pole and signaled the men to row hard; when they were twice as far out, he wanted to shout again, but the men begged him to keep quiet.

barriers.quote: flung it just in front of my ship, so that it came within a little of hitting the end of the rudder
barriers.my_reading: the rock landed very close to the ship and almost struck its steering oar
barriers.note: 'in front of' the ship and 'the end of the rudder' (at the back) seem to contradict each other

barriers.quote: kept the ship off
barriers.my_reading: used the pole to push the ship away from the shore so it did not run aground

barriers.quote: they laid out with a will
barriers.my_reading: they rowed with all their strength
barriers.note: nautical idiom

barriers.quote: I was for jeering at the Cyclops again
barriers.my_reading: I wanted to taunt him again
barriers.note: old idiom

paragraphs.paraphrase: The men plead with Odysseus not to provoke the monster: his first rock drove them back to shore and they thought they were dead, and if he had heard more voices he would have crushed them and the ship with the rocks he can throw so far.

barriers.quote: we made sure it had been the death of us
barriers.my_reading: we were certain it had killed us
barriers.note: 'made sure' in the old sense of 'felt sure', not 'ensured'

paragraphs.paraphrase: Ignoring them, Odysseus angrily shouts his real name: if anyone asks who blinded the Cyclops, he should say it was Odysseus, son of Laertes, of Ithaca.

The Cyclops groans that an old prophecy has come true: the seer Telemus once told him he would be blinded by Odysseus, but he had expected a mighty warrior, not a puny weakling who got him drunk. He invites Odysseus back to receive gifts, promises to ask his father Poseidon to help him on his way, and says only Poseidon can heal his eye.

barriers.quote: Come here, then, Odysseus, that I may make you presents to show my hospitality
barriers.my_reading: a trick to lure Odysseus back within reach
barriers.note: the text does not flag it as a trap; a reader may take it at face value

paragraphs.paraphrase: Odysseus replies that he wishes he were as sure of killing the Cyclops and sending him to the land of the dead as he is that not even Poseidon will heal his eye.

barriers.quote: I wish I could be as sure of killing you outright and sending you down to the house of Hades, as I am that it will take more than Poseidon to cure that eye of yours
barriers.my_reading: I am certain your eye will never be healed, even by Poseidon; I only wish I were as certain I could kill you
barriers.note: the long comparison needs a second reading; 'house of Hades' = the land of the dead

paragraphs.paraphrase: The Cyclops prays to Poseidon: if he is truly his son, let Odysseus never reach home; or, if he must, let him arrive late and wretched, with all his men lost, on someone else's ship, and find trouble in his household.

barriers.quote: the firmament of heaven
barriers.my_reading: the sky
barriers.note: archaic/biblical

barriers.quote: in sore plight
barriers.my_reading: in a wretched condition
barriers.note: archaic

paragraphs.paraphrase: Poseidon heard the prayer. The Cyclops hurled an even bigger rock, which landed just behind the ship, nearly hitting the steering oar, and this time the wave pushed them forward toward the island where the rest of the fleet was waiting.

barriers.quote: Poseidon heard his prayer. Then he picked up a rock
barriers.my_reading: 'he' is the Cyclops, not Poseidon
barriers.note: the nearest name is Poseidon, so for a moment the god seems to be throwing the rock

barriers.quote: toward the shore of the island
barriers.my_reading: the goat island where the other ships were waiting
barriers.note: confirmed in the next paragraph

paragraphs.paraphrase: Back at the goat island the waiting crews, who had been mourning them, welcomed them; they beached the ship, unloaded the Cyclops's sheep and shared them out fairly. The men gave Odysseus the great ram as an extra share, and he sacrificed it to Zeus, burning its thigh bones, but Zeus ignored the offering and was already planning to destroy his ships and men.

barriers.quote: burned its thigh bones to Zeus
barriers.my_reading: burned the thigh bones on the fire as the gods' share of the sacrifice
barriers.note: sacrificial custom not explained

barriers.quote: But he took no heed of my sacrifice, and only thought how he might destroy both my ships and my comrades.
barriers.my_reading: Zeus rejected the offering and was now against Odysseus, presumably because of the blinding and Polyphemus's prayer
barriers.note: the prayer was to Poseidon; why Zeus turns against Odysseus is not explained

paragraphs.paraphrase: They feasted all day and slept on the beach; at dawn they set sail again, grieving for their lost comrades but glad to be alive.

book_level: Stock phrases repeat word for word ('When Dawn, the rosy-fingered child of morning, appeared', 'struck the gray sea with their oars', 'loose the hawsers', 'through the livelong day to the going down of the sun', 'glad to have escaped death though we had lost our comrades'); fine on the page, but they feel antique and very repetitive when heard aloud.

Much of the English reads as early-20th-century British rather than modern: 'should' for 'would' (I should have got home; the four I should have chosen), 'were for staying' / 'was for jeering', 'made sure' for 'felt sure', 'misgave', 'wanted' for 'needed', 'neat milk', 'livelong'.
Sailing and farming vocabulary is left unexplained: hawsers, made fast, run before the gale, breakers, burden, laid out, whey, curdled, kids, yearlings, station, an auger with a wheel and strap.
Customs are assumed rather than explained: guest-gifts and hospitality, suppliants, drink offerings, sacrificing cheese, burning thigh bones, calling the dead three times, mixing wine with water.
The Cyclops is never said to have only one eye; the blinding scene depends on general knowledge of what a Cyclops is.
The Noman / no man trick relies on capitalization; read aloud, the two are identical, so the neighbors' misunderstanding in ¶26-28 is easy to miss.
A few pronouns point the wrong way on first reading: 'Then he picked up a rock' right after Poseidon; Polyphemus calling himself 'your master' and 'him'; the cup-bearer filling 'his cup'.

The gods' motives at the end are unclear: Zeus is presented as the protector of suppliants, yet he rejects Odysseus's sacrifice and plans to destroy his fleet with no stated reason; the link to Poseidon's anger is left implicit.
